content: To effectively compare the performance of various districts in achieving health goals, it is essential to analyze data at the subnational level. Training healthcare providers, facility managers, and data personnel in data analysis, visualization, and utilization is critical for improving data management and use at the facility level. Patient monitoring data can be instrumental in designing training and capacity-building activities by identifying both strengths and weaknesses in facility performance. For instance, facilities with low loss-to-follow-up (LTFU) rates can share their best practices during training sessions, while facilities with identified service delivery gaps can receive targeted training. For example, facilities with low viral load (VL) suppression rates may benefit from additional on-site support and mentoring focused on managing patients on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with high VL. Mentorship from subnational health system levels to facilities can enhance the use of data, including electronic medical record (EMR) reports and tools, to improve clinical management, service delivery, and client tracing. Regular facility data review meetings, held monthly or periodically, can begin with a brief presentation of recent data and trends. These meetings provide opportunities for performance review, information sharing, and reflection on service delivery gaps and weaknesses, encouraging healthcare providers to address these issues. Data staff can present service delivery data and patient alerts during clinical meetings to facilitate discussions on strengths and weaknesses in service delivery, potential interventions for poor outcomes, incomplete or missing data, data backlog or storage issues, and mentoring needs. To support these efforts, health facilities should establish a clear schedule for action reports, specifying who extracts the data, who takes action, who verifies completion, and who clears data reports. Patient monitoring tools should generate actionable reports that clearly define roles and responsibilities for follow-up at each sublevel, ensuring data availability at the appropriate level and clarity in follow-up actions. Analyzing LTFU data is crucial for supporting client tracing efforts. Patients categorized as LTFU often include unidentified deaths, unrecorded transfers, and individuals genuinely lost to follow-up. This information can help determine treatment outcomes and guide re-engagement efforts. Routine analysis of LTFU data should be conducted to understand patient losses and support re-engagement in care. Records should be updated with this information to improve service delivery, adherence, retention, and program reporting. Data can also trigger patient recall through telephone follow-ups and home visits. For example, periodic reviews of patients who have missed appointments or lack antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for more than seven days can identify individuals for recall and tracing interventions. Facilities should review these data to identify actions that could improve patient engagement and experience. Addressing LTFU is particularly important in the context of scaling up differentiated service delivery (DSD) models, such as multi-month dispensing, where tracking patient follow-up status is critical. Routine and timely data reviews at site, district, and national levels can provide insights into transfer-in and transfer-out issues and explain data quality problems. In Cape Town, South Africa, subdistrict meetings are held quarterly to review aggregated patient monitoring data and use the findings to improve service delivery. Challenges and successes in individual clinic performance are highlighted, and possible reasons are addressed through experience sharing and recommendations. For example, using aggregated patient monitoring data, a district identified challenges in early HIV VL testing completion rates across facilities. Clinic C, which performed below average for two consecutive quarters, investigated the reasons for its performance issues by reviewing individual patient records. This process involved extracting ART initiation dates, VL test dates, and results, and analyzing the data after excluding deaths, losses to care, and transfers out. The findings revealed both data errors and missed VL testing opportunities by clinicians. Specific data issues included missing patient folders, discrepancies in ART initiation dates between patient folders and EMRs, VL samples taken outside the appropriate time window, and results not transcribed onto clinic stationery. Most missed VL tests were due to clinicians overlooking testing opportunities, often because of time constraints or high patient loads. To address these issues, the head clinician recommended ongoing in-house training, proper use of patient monitoring tools, regular audits, and avoiding postponing blood sample collection. Clinicians were advised to seek assistance from other staff to ensure VL testing is performed when time is limited. Clerical staff were tasked with organizing patient folders daily, printing test results for patient visits, and capturing and filing test results, including VL. Counselors were instructed to systematically check patient folders and refer patients for VL testing at the appropriate time. The guidance provided in this document outlines steps for adapting and implementing an HIV patient monitoring system, including recommendations for coordinating across programs and transitioning from previous systems to updated ones. The system should meet minimum requirements for quality patient care and be adaptable to specific country settings. Integration of HIV services with other healthcare services, such as antenatal care, tuberculosis care, and chronic disease management, is emphasized. The system should also account for the stage of transition from paper to electronic systems and the adoption of DSD models, ensuring linkage and referral processes are monitored effectively. Sixteen recommended steps for adapting the revised HIV patient monitoring system include forming a technical working group, engaging stakeholders, inventorying current tools, defining indicators and minimum datasets, reviewing digital health ecosystems, adapting tools based on national guidelines, developing training materials, and ensuring sustainability through program budgets and strategic planning. These steps aim to strengthen HIV patient monitoring and care, improve data quality and use, and ensure continuity of care for patients.
